lesson_title: Half a Recipe From Each Parent: How Two Cells Make One Person
hook_text: You started as one cell. It had 46 chromosomes. Neither of your parents gave you 46.
clip_script: Every cell in your body carries a recipe book: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. So how do two parents make one child without doubling the book? Each parent makes special half-cells, the gametes. The sperm carries 23 chromosomes. The egg carries 23. They meet, and 23 plus 23 makes 46, a complete book again, in one cell called the zygote. That was you. Where did that happen? Not in the womb. The sperm are made in the testes, millions every day. The egg is released from an ovary, usually one about every 28 days. They meet in the oviduct, the narrow tube between the ovary and the uterus. Then the ball of cells travels down and settles into the lining of the uterus, the nursery, for about nine months. And because every sperm and every egg picks a different mix of chapters, every child is a new combination. That is why your siblings are not your copies. Half from Ma, half from Pa, all new.
visual_style: An open recipe book with 46 tabs splits into two half books; a sperm and an egg each carry 23 tabs and snap together into one glowing cell; a simple diagram lights up testis, ovary, oviduct and uterus in turn.
pacing: Fast hook, a clear counting beat on 23 plus 23, a quick tour of the organs, a warm finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and name the organ where fertilisation really happens.
